CCGRID has matured into a leading international conference at the intersection of high-performance computing, distributed systems, cloud-edge infrastructure, and energy-aware resource management. It consistently attracts high-quality submissions from both academia and industry, showcasing rigorous, innovative, and impactful work in systems and platforms that are central to modern computing infrastructure.

The conference has been successfully hosted across multiple continents – including Asia, Europe, North America, and Oceania – making it one of the few truly international venues in its domain. This geographic diversity promotes engagement from underrepresented regions and fosters cross-pollination between research communities that might otherwise be siloed. Notably, CCGRID 2026 will be held in Sydney, Australia, reinforcing its deep ties to the Australian research community and its role as a globally recognized conference with Australian branding and leadership influence.
Moreover, CCGRID maintains a strong commitment to diversity, equity, and inclusion, both in speaker representation and reviewer participation. Its community is notably open, collaborative, and welcoming to early-career researchers and students, supporting a wide array of voices and perspectives.
Given its sustained technical excellence, strong academic and industry relevance, and demonstrated global impact, CCGRID fully merits an A ranking in the CORE classification. It plays a unique and essential role among peer conferences by combining applied systems innovation with broad, inclusive engagement and a strong legacy of leadership – including from Australia’s research and systems community.

relationship_to_similar_conferences: DSN intersects with several other A* conferences but differs clearly in scope and focus: - IEEE S&P (Security & Privacy): While both conferences address secure systems, S&P emphasizes theory, cryptographic protocols, and secure system design. DSN instead focuses on system dependability and fault-tolerance, addressing how systems behave under faults and attacks, with an emphasis on resilience and robustness, not just security. - ACM CCS (Computer and Communications Security): CCS is broader in computer security, covering malware, cryptography, access control, etc. DSN, by contrast, emphasizes system-level resilience, fault injection, and recovery techniques, often in operational environments like embedded, cloud, and cyber-physical systems. 6 - USENIX OSDI / ACM SOSP: These are premier venues for operating systems and distributed systems design. While DSN does accept papers on these systems, it evaluates them through the lens of dependability and security, with a strong emphasis on empirical evaluation, fault modeling, and recovery. SOSP/OSDI prioritize system novelty and performance; DSN focuses on system trustworthiness. - SIGMETRICS: Primarily oriented toward performance modeling and quantitative metrics. While DSN also values empirical and analytical rigor, its emphasis is on dependability and resilience, not just system performance. - ISCA (International Symposium on Computer Architecture): ISCA covers architectural innovations, including secure hardware. DSN focuses on evaluating and ensuring the reliability and robustness of those architectures under fault and attack conditions. - RTSS (Real-Time Systems Symposium): RTSS targets timing guarantees and real-time constraints. DSN overlaps in safety-critical systems but primarily evaluates such systems for fault-tolerance, robustness, and resilience, not just timing correctness. In summary, DSN is the only A* venue exclusively centered on dependability and system-level security, bridging both software and hardware domains with an emphasis on fault resilience, experimental validation, and secure system design.
flagship_area_claim: DSN is the flagship conference in the field of dependable and secure computing systems, encompassing both software and hardware reliability, availability, safety, maintainability, and security. It is the premier venue for rigorous, experimental, and theoretical work on fault tolerance, security, resilience, and robustness of systems and networks. DSN is recognized for defining the research agenda in this domain and for consistently featuring high-impact research with real-world relevance, including industrial deployments and advanced academic solutions. The conference has been held annually for over 50 years, backed by strong institutional support (IEEE/IFIP), and is known for its selectivity, long-standing community, and breadth of topics. DSN covers a wide spectrum (i.e., from formal methods to system design, from intrusion detection to software fault injection) making it the most comprehensive and influential venue in this area. No other conference matches DSN’s blend of depth, history, and interdisciplinarity within the dependable systems community.

relationship_to_similar_conferences: EuroSys accepts work across the full spectrum of computer-systems software, from kernels to distributed/cloud platforms and storage, networking, language runtimes, security and emerging hardware interfaces. Here are 5 A* conferences ranked by CORE which are in a similar related area of Systems. SOSP is a single-track, yearly ACM SIGOPS conference that emphasizes fundamental principles and breakthrough concepts in operating and distributed systems; its topical breadth is narrower and its paper volume lower than EuroSys (SOSP’24: 43 vs EuroSys’24: 71; SOSP’23: 35 vs EuroSys’23: 54). OSDI, (USENIX-run conference) likewise focuses on fundamental design-and-implementation contributions with exhaustive empirical evaluation, yet its focus is largely on operating system, cluster software and datacentre infrastructure; EuroSys spans those areas plus additional subsystems and application domains. 7 ASPLOS targets cross-layer papers at the hardware/software boundary—bringint together micro-architecture, compilers and operating systems—so overlap with EuroSys occurs only when the systems-software aspect dominates and the hardware co-design is support rather than primary focus. NSDI focuses heavily around internet- and datacentre-scale network and distributed systems, with a bias towards protocol or service-level experiments; EuroSys welcomes such work but is much more broad. Finally, ISCA is the premier computer architecture venue, accepting work on novel processor and memory-system designs validated by simulation or prototype hardware; EuroSys intersects only when new architectural mechanisms enable qualitatively new systems-software capabilities, but the primary contributions on EuroSys are still tilted towards the software side of systems.
flagship_area_claim: EuroSys is widely regarded within ACM SIGOPS as the premier annual forum for experimentally validated computer-systems research, standing alongside the biennial SOSP and OSDI as the community’s top venues for general-purpose systems software. Its focus span the end-to-end design, implementation, and empirical evaluation of operating system, distributed/cloud/datacentre infrastructures, storage and file systems, networked systems, language/runtime platforms, dependable and secure systems, virtualisation, real-time/embedded platforms, and emerging hardware/software co-designs. In other words, it is the flagship conference for general-purpose systems software. The conference consistently receives 240+ full-papers and regularly attracts 250-300 attendees according to the annual proceedings.

relationship_to_similar_conferences: ACM Multimedia (MM) is a CORE A* cross-disciplinary conference covering multimedia research across diverse domains including video, haptics, virtual and augmented reality, audio, speech, music, sensor data, and social media. While MM encompasses four broad research themes, MMSys has a more specialized focus that aligns with MM’s "multimedia systems" theme. The key relationship is one of scope: MM takes a comprehensive approach to multimedia research spanning theory, applications, and systems, whereas MMSys concentrates exclusively on the systems and infrastructure aspects of multimedia technologies, providing a deeper technical focus on performance, scalability, and implementation challenges within multimedia systems. MM has an acceptance rate comparable to MMSys, with the last few years hovering around 25-27%, (e.g., 26.2% for 2024 [1] 24.6% for 2023 [2]). MM and MMSys serve as complementary venues for multimedia systems research, with their six-month scheduling offset designed to provide researchers with flexible submission opportunities throughout the academic year. NOSSDAV is recognized with a B ranking in CORE.

relationship_to_similar_conferences: The DAC conference ( https://www.dac.com/About/About-DAC) is in a broadly similar general area; however, DAC focuses on hardware and system design, whereas the scope of RTSS is specialised to systems that support real-time behaviour (i.e. where the combination of software and hardware is required to complete specific functionality within a well-defined timeframe). The POPL conference ( https://popl24.sigplan.org/) is also in a broadly similar area. POPL however focuses on programming languages and the functional behaviour of software. This is in contrast to RTSS, which focused on the timing behaviour of real-time computing systems.
flagship_area_claim: RTSS is widely recognised as the flagship conference in "Real-Time Systems". The real-time systems community supports a number of conferences, including RTSS, RTAS, ECRTS, RTNS, and RTCSA. RTSS is by some considerable margin the top conference in this field as measured in terms of number of submissions, acceptance rate, and participation. It is the one that all of the top people in real-time systems aim to publish in. This has been the case for at least 30 years (arguably since the conference’s inception 45 years ago) and continues to be the case today. RTSS benefits from the highest quality governance (via IEEE Technical Community on Real-Time Systems (TCRTS) https://cmte.ieee.org/tcrts/) and transparency https://cmte.ieee.org/tcrts/conferences/transparency/
other_relevant_info: The real-time systems field is large enough to support a hierarchy of conferences, with RTSS as the flagship, underpinned by RTAS which has a tighter focus on practice, then ECRTS, RTNS, and RTCSA. The community is however smaller in comparison to other fields. This is reflected in the level of citations and hence the h-indices of the top researchers in real-time systems, with the 20th person listed having a h-index of 56. In general, highly experienced and successful researchers who have worked in this field for 20+ years have a h-index of around 40. The size of the community also has an impact on the h5-index of the conferences.

flagship_area_claim: Why SenSys is a Flagship (A*) Conference and Its Research Area The ACM Conference on Embedded Networked Sensor Systems (SenSys) is the flagship conference in the area of intelligent sensing and embedded systems, particularly at the intersection of networked sensing, embedded computing, wireless/mobile systems, and AI-driven applications. It serves as the top venue for research that tightly integrates physical sensing, in-sensor intelligence, and real-world deployments, addressing critical challenges in cyber-physical systems, mobile edge intelligence, and ubiquitous computing. Specific Research Area SenSys leads the research area of embedded artificial intelligence and intelligent sensing systems – a domain shaped by the convergence of: Cyber-physical systems and embedded platforms Edge AI and in-sensor computation Low-power wireless and mobile communication Sensor-driven data systems and distributed intelligence IoT and smart environments This area is distinct yet complementary to fields like mobile computing, embedded systems, and wireless networking. SenSys fills a unique and critical niche by emphasizing end-to-end systems research with real-world deployment. Why SenSys Qualifies as a Flagship (A*) Conference Unified, High-Impact Scope Beginning in 2026, SenSys consolidates the research communities of SenSys, IPSN (a CORE A* conference), and IoTDI into a single flagship event, co-sponsored by ACM and IEEE. This unification reflects the community’s desire for a premier venue that spans sensing, systems, and embedded intelligence. Highly Selective and Prestigious SenSys maintains a low acceptance rate (typically ~15-20%), reflecting a strong commitment to research quality and innovation. It attracts leading academic and industry contributions with global reach. Large and Diverse Research Community The conference serves a substantial and interdisciplinary community that spans sensor networks, embedded systems, AI for the edge, robotics, environmental sensing, and ubiquitous computing. This breadth supports sustained growth and engagement across disciplines. Systems-Centric and Deployment-Focused Unlike theory- or simulation-focused venues, SenSys is distinct in its emphasis on real-world deployment, system design, and hardware-software integration. It prioritizes empirical validation, scalability, and practical constraints. Proven Research Impact Over the years, SenSys has been the venue for seminal work in areas such as energy-efficient sensing, RF localization, low-power system design, in-sensor machine learning, and distributed embedded algorithms, many of which have shaped research and product development in academia and industry.

flagship_area_claim: The Design Automation Conference (DAC) is the premier event for electronic design and automation professionals, researchers, and academics. It is considered the flagship conference in the area of design automation, chips, and systems. With its top-notch research track, its exhibition, engineering track, and young fellows programs, DAC brings together designers and design automation users, researcher, s and vendors as well as specialists in the hardware and software design, test and manufacturing of electronic circuits and systems. It assembles the ecosystem’s foremost leaders, enabling them to spotlight breakthroughs pushing boundaries in the field. DAC is dedicated to exploring advances in the design and automation of electronic systems, covering areas such as EDA tools, AI, machine learning, IP, embedded systems, hardware security, and more. With over 60 years of history, DAC provides a unique opportunity for collaboration among those leading the way in the development of chips, systems, and software for electronics innovation. Both its sister conference in Europe, DATE, and the smaller, but high-quality ICCAD, have all seen enormous success and growth in the past few years and look to DAC as the flagship to emulate. DAC is an extremely competitive conference, with acceptance rates always around 22% to 25%.

flagship_area_claim: CAV is the premier international conference on computer-aided verification.It provides a forum for a broad range of advanced research in areas ranging model checking and automated theorem proving to testing, synthesis, and related fields. Research reported in CAV includes the application of formal methods to many kinds of systems, including hardware, software, neural networks, and communication protocols. It covers many system models, including finite-state and infinite state systems, hybrid systems and probabilistic systems. It encompasses both theory, tools, and industrial case studies. The common thread is the use of automation to help designers build more reliable systems.
